lead: A microstrip patch antenna is a flat piece of copper printed on one side of a thin dielectric board, with a solid copper ground on the other side. The patch and the ground form a cavity that resonates when the patch is about half a wavelength long in the board, and the field that fringes out at two of its edges radiates. It costs almost nothing to etch with the rest of a circuit, so it sits in phones, Wi-Fi routers, GPS receivers, FASTag readers and radar panels. Its price is a narrow band and modest gain.
prereq: You need: the microstrip line and its effective permittivity from the transmission-line topic, and gain and polarization from the antenna fundamentals topic.

blocks.text: A rectangular patch has length L (the resonant dimension) and width W, on a substrate of thickness h and relative permittivity ε<sub>r</sub>. In the dominant TM<sub>10</sub> mode the electric field under the patch is vertical, with a half-cosine variation along L: strongest at the two edges a distance L apart, zero at the centre line, and of opposite sign at the two ends.

At each of those two edges the field fringes out of the board. At the edge where it points down it runs from the patch out to the ground beyond; at the edge where it points up it runs from the ground back in to the patch. Seen from above, both horizontal parts therefore point the same way, while the vertical parts are opposite and cancel in the far field. The two edges act as two narrow slots radiating in phase, a broadside pair about half a guided wavelength apart, with the beam straight up from the board and the polarization along L. The two side edges along L radiate little.

The substrate decides size and band. A higher ε<sub>r</sub> shrinks the patch; a thicker board with low ε<sub>r</sub> (foam, ε<sub>r</sub> ≈ 1.1) widens the band and raises the efficiency but launches more surface wave. On 1.6 mm FR-4 (ε<sub>r</sub> ≈ 4.4) a 2.4 GHz patch has a band of only about 1 to 3 % and a gain of about 5 to 7 dBi.

The model treats the patch as a short length of wide microstrip line, open at both ends. The fringing makes each end look longer by ΔL, so resonance needs L + 2ΔL = λ<sub>g</sub>/2, where λ<sub>g</sub> = λ<sub>0</sub>/√ε<sub>eff</sub>. Design in this order:

blocks.where: W is the width in m for good radiation efficiency; c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s; f is the design frequency in Hz. This step uses ε<sub>r</sub>, not ε<sub>eff</sub>.

blocks.text: ε<sub>eff</sub> is the effective permittivity, between 1 and ε<sub>r</sub> because part of the field is in air.
ΔL is the extra length added by the fringing field at one open end, in m (Hammerstad’s formula).

blocks.where: L is the physical patch length in m.

blocks.text: The input resistance is highest at a radiating edge (a few hundred ohms on a thin board) and falls toward zero at the centre. A simple estimate takes one radiating slot of conductance G<sub>1</sub> ≈ W/(120λ<sub>0</sub>) for W < λ<sub>0</sub>, so the edge resistance is R<sub>edge</sub> ≈ 1/(2G<sub>1</sub>); coupling between the two slots lowers the true value somewhat. A feed point moved in by y<sub>0</sub> sees R(y<sub>0</sub>) = R<sub>edge</sub> cos²(πy<sub>0</sub>/L).

An inset microstrip feed cuts a notch so the line meets the patch at the 50 Ω point; it is printed with the patch but its line radiates a little. A coaxial probe comes up through the ground to the 50 Ω point; on a thick board the long probe adds series inductance that detunes the match, so thick designs add a capacitive gap or an L-shaped probe. An aperture-coupled feed couples through a slot in the ground from a line on a second board, which keeps feed radiation away from the patch.

Feeding the patch at two points on adjacent sides with equal amplitude and 90° phase difference, or trimming two opposite corners, makes it circularly polarized, which is how GPS patches are built. Patches are combined into arrays exactly as in uniform linear arrays, usually spaced about λ0/2 and fed by a printed corporate network; tapered and steered versions follow phased arrays.

examples.question: Design a rectangular patch for 2.4 GHz on FR-4 with ε<sub>r</sub> = 4.4 and h = 1.6 mm. Find W, ε<sub>eff</sub>, ΔL and L, and check the resonant frequency.
examples.answer: W ≈ 38.0 mm, ε<sub>eff</sub> ≈ 4.09, ΔL ≈ 0.74 mm, L ≈ 29.4 mm; the patch resonates at 2.40 GHz in the TM<sub>10</sub> mode, about 0.24λ<sub>0</sub> long.

examples.question: For the same patch, estimate the edge resistance with the single-slot model and the inset depth y<sub>0</sub> for a 50 Ω feed.
steps: cos²(πy<sub>0</sub>/L) = 50/197 = 0.2537, so cos(πy<sub>0</sub>/L) = 0.5037 and πy<sub>0</sub>/L = 1.0435 rad.
y<sub>0</sub> = 1.0435 × 29.44/π = 9.78 mm from the radiating edge.
A 50 Ω microstrip line on this board is about 3.0 mm wide; leave a gap of about 1 mm either side of it in the notch.
examples.answer: R<sub>edge</sub> ≈ 197 Ω and an inset of about 9.8 mm brings the feed to 50 Ω. Because slot coupling lowers R<sub>edge</sub>, a simulator usually trims the inset by a millimetre or two.

traps: Making L = λ<sub>0</sub>/2. The wave is slowed by the board: use λ<sub>g</sub> = λ<sub>0</sub>/√ε<sub>eff</sub> and subtract 2ΔL; λ<sub>0</sub>/2 would give 62.5 mm instead of 29.4 mm.
Putting ε<sub>eff</sub> into the width formula. W uses ε<sub>r</sub>; ε<sub>eff</sub> is for the guided wavelength and ΔL.
Feeding at the edge with a 50 Ω line. The edge is a few hundred ohms; move the feed in by y<sub>0</sub> or use a quarter-wave transformer.
Saying the two radiating edges are out of phase so the patch cannot radiate broadside. The vertical fields are opposite, but the horizontal fringing fields that radiate point the same way.
Calling a thick foam patch free of drawbacks. It gains band but loses to probe inductance, surface waves and a larger patch.

quiz.q: Name the layers of a microstrip patch antenna and the job of each.
quiz.a: Patch: resonates and radiates from two edges. Substrate: holds the field and sets the electrical size. Ground plane: completes the cavity and stops radiation to the back.

quiz.q: Why is L shorter than half the guided wavelength?
quiz.a: The fringing field makes each open end look ΔL longer, so L + 2ΔL = λ<sub>g</sub>/2 and L is 2ΔL shorter.

quiz.q: Find W for a 5 GHz patch on ε<sub>r</sub> = 2.2.
Why does ε<sub>eff</sub> lie between 1 and ε<sub>r</sub>?
quiz.a: Part of the field is in the board and part in the air above it, so the wave sees a weighted mix of the two permittivities.

quiz.q: An edge resistance of 240 Ω must be brought to 50 Ω on a 30 mm patch. Find the inset depth.
A designer doubles the substrate height of a working patch. Give two effects and one correction.
quiz.a: The band widens because the cavity Q falls; ΔL grows and ε<sub>eff</sub> shifts, so the resonance moves down. Shorten L to retune, recheck the feed point, and watch for surface-wave loss and probe inductance.

quiz.q: Compare an inset feed and a probe feed on a 3 mm foam substrate.
quiz.a: The probe reaches the 50 Ω point from below without a notch and keeps the feed line off the radiating side, but a 3 mm probe adds inductance that must be tuned out. An inset line on foam needs a wide 50 Ω line and a deep notch, and the line itself radiates.

beyond: Not for the exam. Millimetre-wave 5G phones hide small patch arrays in modules a few millimetres across, and stacked or slotted patches (E-shaped, U-slot) reach 20 to 30 % bandwidth. Cavity-model and full-wave analysis replace the transmission-line model when accuracy matters. Search for cavity model of a patch, U-slot patch, stacked patch and antenna-in-package.

figure.caption: The 2.4 GHz patch of the worked examples on 1.6 mm FR-4. Top view to scale: 29.4 mm by 38.0 mm, with the 50 Ω line inset 9.8 mm into the radiating edge. Side view: the field points down at one radiating edge and up at the other, yet the fringing field runs from patch to ground on one side and from ground to patch on the other, so seen from above both horizontal parts point the same way and the two edges radiate in phase.
